thread.title: Is Facebook Facing A Perfect Storm?

author: TipRanks
title: Is Facebook Facing A Perfect Storm?
text:
Way back in 1991 when a nor'easter collided with the remnants of Hurricane Grace off the coast of New England, the combined system expanded back to hurricane strength and sank the fishing boat, Andrea Gail . You've probably seen the movie, The Perfect Storm , with George Clooney and Mark Wahlberg.
That famous storm was a fluke, caused by an unusual and unlikely combination of weather systems colliding all at once. Facebook, Inc. ( FB - Research Report ), the $380 billion social media behemoth, looks like it may be facing its own perfect storm, as a series of public relations crises, Zuckerberg gaffes, and stock sell-offs have struck the company in succession over recent months. We'll review the news and dive into TipRanks data on the company's share price history, to get a sense of where Facebook is headed, and if it has a way out of its current problems.
Troubles Begin with Privacy Start back in March. News broke that the British data mining and political consulting firm had, without company permission or user consent, harvested personal data from several million Facebook user personal profiles and then allowed the data to be used for political purposes. By April, the outcry was loud enough to bring Facebook founder and chairman Mark Zuckerberg into the hot seat before Congress, where he gave five hours of testimony that completely and utterly failed to ease public concerns.
It wasn't that he said the wrong things - Zuckerberg took responsibility for the scandal, as head of Facebook and announced that he was taking measures to prevent a recurrence. Well and good. His bigger problem came in the realm of PR. He made several statements which Congress and the public took to mean that he values his own privacy more than that of Facebook users - an unforgivable gaffe in this day of online security concerns. In addition, his demeanor throughout the testimony was described as 'flat' and 'robotic.' He was compared - not favorably - to the android character Data, from Star Trek . In an ironic twist, Facebook became the platform of choice to share the resulting memes.
The spring-time crisis for Facebook was visible in the stock market. Between March 16 and March 27, the company's stock fell from $185 to $152. It began turning back up on a combination of the short public attention span, relief that Zuckerberg's Congressional testimony was out of the way, and the underlying strength of Facebook's advertising revenue stream. By July 25, Facebook was trading at $217 per share.
Disappointing Quarterly Earnings And then, the Q2 earnings report came out, and the stock dropped almost 25%, to $176 per share, wiping $120 billion off the books in one day.
The rout came on the heels of slight misses in total revenue, earnings per share, and daily active users (DAUs). Revenue came in at $13.23 billion compared to the $13.36 billion estimate, EPS was off by 2 cents, and DAUs were reported as 1.47 billion against the estimate of 1.49 billion. Average revenue per user was actually up by 2 cents.
The DAU number was the most dangerous for Facebook. Social media depends on constant acquisition of new users to maintain the networks and keep the ad revenue coming in; if a social media company cannot continue building its user base, it will rapidly go the way of Google+. Facebook is hardly facing that, but the slowdown in DAU was enough to spook investors. Even though the gross numbers were good, the trend was enough to make people worry.
Continuing Concerns about Privacy In recent weeks, the barrage of bad press and publicity has kept up. The New York Times last week published a 6,100-word article on Facebook's two-year-running and ongoing attempts to avoid blame for alleged Russian election interference using its social platform. The Times described the company's strategy as 'deny, delay, or deflect,' and claims that top Facebook execs are working to keep information from the company board as well as the general public.
Zuckerberg's propensity for gaffes was on display in his response to the Times article. Commenting on the subject of Definers Public Affairs, a PR firm which the paper alleges collected dirt on Facebook's critics and competition - Zuckerberg said that he only knew about it when he saw it in the paper. It was a denial reminiscent of President Obama's claim not to know about the Clinton email scandal until he saw it on TV, with the difference being that Zuckerberg comes across as less personable than Obama, and so less believable when asserting the implausible.
The Gaffes Keep Coming It's not just major political issues that are hurting Facebook, though. Smaller missteps have been dogging the company in the past month.
Facebook rolled out an automatic comment system - not a bad thing, in itself - and the initial test was on live video posts. The timing, however, could not have been worse, as the new feature debuted in the aftermath of the horrific synagogue shooting in Pittsburgh. Being able to select 'So sad,' or 'This is horrible' just didn't sit well with the public, and the feature was quickly removed. The company said only, "We have been testing a suggested comment feature on Live videos. Clearly, this wasn't implemented properly and we have disabled the feature for now."
Also recently, and possibly just as petty, Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) head Tim Cook gave an interview to MSNBC in which he said a few things critical of Facebook and its 'traffic in your personal life.' Zuckerberg was reportedly unhappy about it - so unhappy that he ordered all Facebook managers to switch to Android smartphones. The company has denied it, but it still doesn't look good when a report surfaces that Facebook is meddling in employees' personal lives - in response to criticisms on personal privacy issues!
All of this, taken together, explains why employee satisfaction is down at Facebook. In a recent survey of Facebook workers, 52% said they were optimistic about the company's future, and 53% said that Facebook makes the world a better place. Those numbers were 84% and 72% one year ago. Seems that a constant barrage of bad news can deliver a hit on morale as well as on the stock price.
Is There Reason for Optimism? It won't do to count Facebook out. The company has undeniable strengths: a massive user base, global reach, a highly profitable advertising model, and a strong revenue stream. The Q3 earnings report showed a large beat in earnings per share (almost 20% higher than estimates), but the daily and monthly active user numbers continued to slip. Average revenue per user met expectations. In the earnings call, Zuckerberg said that moving forward, the company will focus on better matching costs and revenues. Facebook's greatest strength, however, is in the number 2.6 billion - the number of regular users on its family of apps: Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram, and Messenger.
Market analysts mostly agree. A few weeks ago, Argus analyst Joseph Bonner ( Track Record & Ratings ) raised his price target on FB to $260 on a 'Buy' rating. More recently, Stifel's Scott Devitt ( Track Record & Ratings ) discounted the probability that Zuckerberg will be forced out of Facebook's leadership. He says FB's "campaign trail to rebuild credibility will be long and difficult," and added that management changes "would be viewed positively by the vast majority of constituents." Devitt kept a 'Buy' rating, although he did not give a specific price target.
The analyst consensus on Facebook remains a 'Strong Buy,' with the average price target of $188 representing a 42% upside from the current share price of $132. The bottom line: You can't write off a company with 2.6 billion users worldwide and a $380 billion market cap.
